work.title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde

passageLocation.chapter: Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case
passageLocation.openingWords: With every day, and from both

text: With every day, and from both sides of my intelligence, the moral and the intellectual, I thus drew steadily nearer to that truth, by whose partial discovery I have been doomed to such a dreadful shipwreck: that man is not truly one, but truly two. I say two, because the state of my own knowledge does not pass beyond that point. Others will follow, others will outstrip me on the same lines; and I hazard the guess that man will be ultimately known for a mere polity of multifarious, incongruous and independent denizens.

curation.context: Near the end of Stevenson’s 1886 novella, Henry Jekyll sets down his account of the divided self he sought to understand.
curation.rationale: Truth, discovery, shipwreck, divided intelligence and a crowd of inner denizens make identity spatial and unstable. The passage supports poems of doubleness without requiring the novel's plot.
